title: Congeners in Alcohol: What They Are and Which Drinks Have the Most
excerpt: Congeners are the chemicals in your drink besides ethanol: methanol, acetaldehyde, fusel oils, and tannins. Here's what they are, a ladder of drinks from lowest to highest, and what the best study says about their role in hangovers.
metaDescription: What congeners in alcohol are, which drinks have the most, and what the bourbon vs. vodka study shows about how much they really affect hangovers.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** congeners are the small amounts of other chemicals, besides ethanol, that end up in an alcoholic drink during fermentation, distillation, and aging. They include methanol, acetaldehyde, fusel oils (heavier alcohols), esters, and tannins. They give dark spirits and red wine much of their flavor, color, and aroma. Research suggests they can also make a hangover feel worse at the same amount of alcohol, which is why bourbon, brandy, and red wine have a worse reputation than vodka or gin.

**What congeners don't do:** they are not the main cause of a hangover. The amount of ethanol you drink matters far more than the type of drink. In the best-known controlled study, people who drank vodka still had hangovers; bourbon just made them a bit worse. Choosing a low-congener drink can take the edge off. It won't save you from drinking too much.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on alcohol and hangovers. It isn't a substitute for advice from a doctor who knows your health history. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US, or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222) if** someone has blurred or lost vision, severe stomach pain, confusion, trouble breathing, or seizures after drinking, especially after drinking homemade, unlabeled, or suspiciously cheap spirits. These can be signs of methanol poisoning, which is a medical emergency and has nothing to do with an ordinary hangover.

## What Are Congeners? The Dictionary Definition

The word **congener** (pronounced *KON-juh-ner*) comes from Latin and means "of the same kind." In general English it can mean any thing or organism that belongs to the same group as another. Biologists use it for species in the same genus, and chemists and pharmacologists use it for compounds that are closely related to each other.

When people talk about **congeners in alcohol**, they mean something more specific: **every biologically active compound in a drink other than ethanol (the alcohol you are drinking for) and water.** They're by-products. Yeast makes most of them while it ferments sugar into alcohol. Distillation concentrates or strips some of them out. Barrel aging adds more as the spirit draws compounds out of the wood.

Congeners are usually present in tiny amounts compared with ethanol. But "tiny" is relative. Many of them are what give whiskey its smoke and caramel, red wine its dryness, and rum its molasses depth. A drink with no congeners at all would be close to pure ethanol and water, which is roughly what a well-filtered vodka aims to be.

### Congeners vs. other things in your drink

It helps to separate congeners from a few things that often get lumped in with them:

- **Sulfites** are mostly added as preservatives, especially to wine. They aren't congeners in the strict sense. They matter for people with sulfite sensitivity (often people with asthma), but there's little evidence they cause ordinary hangover headaches.
- **Sugar and mixers** aren't congeners either. Sweet mixers can make you drink faster, which raises the total alcohol you take in.
- **Histamine and other biogenic amines** form during fermentation, particularly in red wine. Some writers count them as congeners and some don't. They may play a part in wine headaches for some people, though the evidence is mixed. Our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) covers that in more detail.

## The Main Types of Congeners

There are hundreds of congeners across different drinks. A handful get most of the attention because they're the most studied or most plausible as hangover contributors.

### Methanol

Methanol is the simplest alcohol, and the one with the scariest reputation. In legitimate drinks it's present in small amounts. It comes mainly from **pectin**, a substance in fruit skins and cell walls, which breaks down during fermentation. That's why fruit-based drinks tend to have more of it. Fruit brandies and some red wines are at the higher end, while grain spirits like vodka usually have very little.

Here's why methanol is interesting for hangovers. Your body breaks methanol down using the same enzyme it uses for ethanol (alcohol dehydrogenase). That enzyme prefers ethanol. So as long as ethanol is in your blood, methanol mostly waits in line. Once the ethanol has cleared, the enzyme gets to the methanol and turns it into **formaldehyde** and then **formic acid**, both of which are toxic.

Some researchers have pointed out that this timing lines up with the hangover, which peaks around when blood alcohol returns to zero. That's one proposed reason dark, fruit-based drinks might produce worse mornings. It's also the most plausible explanation for why "hair of the dog" seems to help briefly: a fresh drink pushes methanol breakdown back again. That doesn't make it a good idea. It just delays the problem and adds more alcohol for your liver to process.

To be clear about scale: the methanol in normal, commercially made drinks is far below toxic levels. Methanol *poisoning* comes from badly made or deliberately adulterated spirits, sometimes sold as cheap or counterfeit brand-name bottles, particularly in places with weak regulation. That's a medical emergency, not a hangover. Doctors actually use ethanol or a drug called fomepizole as antidotes because both block the enzyme from turning methanol into its toxic products.

### Acetaldehyde

Acetaldehyde is a special case. Small amounts are present in some drinks as a congener, especially in some wines and in drinks that have been exposed to air. But the vast majority of the acetaldehyde in your body after drinking is made **by your own liver** when it breaks down ethanol.

Acetaldehyde is toxic. It's behind the facial flushing, racing heart, and nausea that people with the ALDH2 gene variant get, which we explain in our [Asian flush guide](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive). It has long been suspected as a hangover contributor, though studies haven't shown a clean link between acetaldehyde levels the next morning and how bad the hangover feels. Because most of it comes from ethanol itself, the acetaldehyde you swallow in the glass is a minor factor compared with the acetaldehyde your body makes from the alcohol.

### Fusel oils (higher alcohols)

"Fusel" comes from an old German word for bad liquor. Fusel oils are a group of **heavier alcohols**, including isoamyl alcohol, isobutanol, and propanol. Yeast makes them from amino acids during fermentation, and more of them form when fermentation runs warm or fast.

They have a strong, solvent-like smell in large amounts, and in small amounts they add body and character. Distillers control them by deciding which parts of each distillation run to keep. Spirits distilled to very high purity, like vodka, have most fusel oils removed. Spirits bottled at lower distillation strength to keep their flavor, like many whiskeys, rums, and brandies, keep more.

Fusel oils are often blamed for hangovers. The idea is plausible because they're broken down by some of the same enzymes as ethanol and can have their own effects on the nervous system. But the human evidence that fusel oils specifically drive hangovers is thin. It's fairer to say they're part of the overall congener load that seems to make hangovers worse.

### Tannins and other polyphenols

Tannins are plant compounds that cause the dry, mouth-puckering feel of red wine and strong tea. In wine they come mostly from grape skins, seeds, and stems, and from oak. In aged spirits like whiskey, bourbon, and cognac, they come mainly from the barrel.

Tannins have been linked to headaches in some people, possibly through effects on serotonin, but the research is limited and inconsistent. They're one reason red wine gets blamed for headaches more than white wine, alongside histamine and the simple fact that red wine is often stronger than people assume.

### Esters, aldehydes, and the rest

The fruity, floral notes in many drinks come from **esters**, formed when acids and alcohols combine. Other aldehydes such as furfural come from heating and from charred barrels. These compounds are mostly about flavor. There's little research on their individual role in hangovers, so they're best thought of as part of the overall congener content rather than separate culprits.

## The Congener Ladder: Which Drinks Have the Most

Congener levels vary by brand, production method, and aging, so any ranking is approximate. But the general pattern is consistent across sources: **clear, highly distilled spirits sit at the bottom and dark, aged, or fruit-based drinks sit at the top.**

Here's the rough order, from lowest to highest congener content:

| Rank | Drink | Why it sits here |
|------|-------|------------------|
| 1 (lowest) | Vodka | Distilled to very high purity and often filtered, which strips most congeners |
| 2 | Gin | Neutral grain spirit plus botanicals; low congeners, a few extra flavor compounds |
| 3 | White (light) rum | Usually filtered and lightly aged |
| 4 | Blanco tequila (100% agave) | Unaged, but agave fermentation leaves more character than vodka |
| 5 | Beer and white wine | Not distilled, but moderate congeners; white wine has fewer tannins than red |
| 6 | Whiskey (Scotch, rye, Irish) | Distilled to lower strength and aged in wood |
| 7 | Bourbon | New charred oak barrels add lots of wood-derived compounds |
| 8 | Dark and aged rum | Molasses base plus barrel aging |
| 9 | Red wine | Tannins, histamine, and more methanol from grape skins |
| 10 (highest) | Brandy and cognac | Fruit base (more methanol) plus long barrel aging |

A few honest caveats:

- **Within each category there's a wide range.** A cheap, quickly made whiskey and a carefully distilled one can differ a lot. So can a 100% agave tequila and a "mixto" tequila that uses other sugars. Our [tequila hangover guide](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) goes into why that difference matters.
- **Beer and wine are lower in alcohol per serving,** so per drink you're also getting less ethanol. Congener content per ounce isn't the whole story.
- **Flavored and sweetened products** add their own variables that aren't captured in this list.

One older British study, often cited in reviews (Pawan, 1973, *Proceedings of the Nutrition Society*), asked volunteers to rate hangovers after different drinks and found a similar order, with brandy and red wine at the worst end and gin and vodka at the mildest. It was small and done decades ago, so treat it as supporting evidence rather than proof.

## The Bourbon vs. Vodka Study: What the Best Evidence Shows

The most useful study on congeners and hangovers is a controlled trial led by Damaris Rohsenow at Brown University, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010.

**What they did.** The researchers recruited healthy young adults, mostly in their twenties, who were heavy but not dependent drinkers. Over separate overnight sessions in a lab, participants drank either bourbon, vodka, or a placebo, dosed to reach a fairly high blood alcohol level (around 0.11 g%, above the US driving limit). The bourbon they used had many times more congeners than the vodka. They slept in the lab and were tested the next morning on how they felt, how they slept, and how they performed on attention and reaction-time tasks.

**What they found.**

- **Bourbon produced worse hangovers than vodka.** People rated their hangover as more severe after bourbon, at the same blood alcohol level.
- **Both drinks caused hangovers.** Vodka was not hangover-free. Compared with placebo, both bourbon and vodka disrupted sleep and caused hangover symptoms.
- **Next-day performance was impaired by both, about equally.** Alcohol worsened attention and reaction time the next morning, but the type of drink didn't make a meaningful difference to that impairment.

**What it means.** Congeners appear to make you *feel* worse the morning after, but the alcohol itself does most of the damage, including the parts you may not notice, like slower reactions. That second point matters. Someone who drank vodka might feel better than a bourbon drinker and assume they're fine to drive or work. The study suggests their performance may be just as impaired.

The same research group also published a review of the evidence on beverage congeners (Rohsenow and Howland, *Current Drug Abuse Reviews*, 2010). Its overall conclusion fits the trial: congeners seem to add to hangover severity, but they're a secondary factor after the amount of ethanol consumed.

## Why Congeners Might Make Hangovers Worse

Nobody has fully mapped how congeners add to a hangover, partly because hangovers themselves aren't fully understood. Our [hangover science hub](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025) covers the bigger picture. For congeners specifically, the main ideas are:

1. **Delayed toxic breakdown products.** As described above, methanol is converted into formaldehyde and formic acid after ethanol clears, roughly when hangovers peak.
2. **Extra work for the same enzymes.** Many congeners are processed by the same liver enzymes that handle ethanol, which may slow clearance or prolong exposure to by-products.
3. **Inflammation.** Hangovers are associated with signs of an inflammatory response in the body. Some researchers think congeners could add to that, though direct human evidence is limited.
4. **Individual effects of specific compounds.** Tannins, histamine, and certain other compounds may trigger headaches in people who are sensitive to them.

None of these mechanisms is proven to be the main driver. The honest summary is that congeners are a reasonable explanation for why some drinks feel worse than others, and the bourbon vs. vodka trial supports that, but the details are still being worked out.

## Congeners by Drink: What to Know

### Vodka

Vodka is the lowest-congener drink you can buy, which is why it's often recommended as the "cleanest" choice. That's true as far as congeners go. But vodka is easy to drink fast and mix into sweet drinks, so people often end up drinking more of it. Our [vodka hangover guide](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains why vodka still gives plenty of people bad mornings.

### Whiskey and bourbon

Whiskey keeps more congeners from both distillation and wood aging. Bourbon is required to be aged in new charred oak containers, which adds a lot of wood-derived compounds, and it's the drink used in the main congener study. Scotch, rye, and Irish whiskey vary widely. See our [whiskey hangover guide](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) for drink-specific tips.

### Tequila

Tequila's reputation is mixed. A good 100% agave blanco is relatively low in congeners, while aged tequilas (reposado and añejo) pick up more from barrels, and cheaper "mixto" tequilas can be rougher. Some of tequila's bad reputation probably comes from how it's usually drunk: in shots, quickly, at parties.

### Rum

Light rum is fairly low in congeners. Dark and aged rums, made from molasses and often aged for years, are near the top of the ladder. Our [rum health analysis](/never-hungover/rum-health-analysis-complete-spirits-impact-study-2025) covers the differences between styles.

### Wine

Red wine has more tannins, more histamine, and usually more methanol than white wine, because the juice spends time in contact with grape skins. White and sparkling wines are lower in congeners, but sparkling wine's bubbles may speed up alcohol absorption. Our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) and [champagne hangover guide](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) cover both.

### Beer

Beer sits in the middle. It isn't distilled, so it keeps fermentation congeners, but it's much weaker per serving than spirits. Darker and stronger craft beers tend to have more congeners than light lagers. If you've heard that the order you drink beer and liquor matters, our piece on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) explains why the total amount you drink matters more than the sequence.

## Does Choosing Low-Congener Drinks Actually Help?

Somewhat. If you're going to drink a set amount, choosing vodka, gin, or a clear spirit instead of bourbon, brandy, or red wine will probably give you a milder hangover, based on the controlled evidence available. That's a real, if modest, benefit.

But it has limits, and it's worth being direct about them:

- **It doesn't prevent a hangover.** Vodka drinkers in the Brown University study still had hangovers.
- **It doesn't protect your performance.** Next-day attention and reaction time were impaired about equally by both drinks.
- **It doesn't make heavy drinking safer.** Congeners have nothing to do with the liver, heart, and brain risks of drinking a lot of ethanol.
- **It can backfire.** If "clean" drinks lead you to drink more, the extra ethanol will easily outweigh any congener benefit.

The things that make the biggest difference are still the basic ones: drink less in total, pace yourself (roughly one standard drink per hour at most), eat before and while drinking, alternate with water, and give yourself time to sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through all of these in order of how much they help.

## Where DHM Fits In (And Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol, mostly in animal research. The leading ideas are that it may affect how alcohol acts on GABA receptors in the brain and may support the enzymes that clear alcohol and acetaldehyde. Human data are still limited, and our [honest DHM review](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) goes through what is and isn't known.

What matters for this article: **there's no evidence that DHM breaks down or neutralizes congeners like methanol, fusel oils, or tannins.** Its proposed effects are on ethanol and acetaldehyde, which, as the bourbon vs. vodka study showed, is where most of the hangover comes from anyway. So the two approaches don't compete. Choosing lower-congener drinks reduces one smaller contributor; DHM is aimed at the larger one, with evidence that's promising but not settled.

If you want to try DHM, a plain single-ingredient option like [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple place to start, and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts. It isn't a license to drink more, and it won't undo the effects of drinking heavily. If you take prescription medicines or have a liver condition, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Congeners are the non-ethanol compounds in alcoholic drinks: methanol, acetaldehyde, fusel oils, tannins, esters, and many more. They're responsible for much of the flavor of dark spirits and red wine, and the best controlled evidence shows they make hangovers feel worse at the same blood alcohol level. Vodka and gin sit at the bottom of the congener ladder; bourbon, dark rum, red wine, and brandy sit at the top.

But the type of drink is the smaller lever. The amount of alcohol is the bigger one. Pick a cleaner drink if you like, and then drink less of it, more slowly, with food and water.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What are congeners in alcohol?**

Congeners are the chemical compounds in an alcoholic drink other than ethanol and water. They're made during fermentation, changed by distillation, and added during barrel aging. Common examples are methanol, acetaldehyde, fusel oils (heavier alcohols like isoamyl alcohol), esters, and tannins. They provide much of a drink's flavor, aroma, and color.

**Which alcohol has the fewest congeners?**

Vodka has the fewest congeners because it's distilled to very high purity and usually filtered. Gin, light rum, and 100% agave blanco tequila are also relatively low. Brandy, cognac, red wine, bourbon, and dark rum are at the high end.

**Do congeners cause hangovers?**

They contribute, but they aren't the main cause. In a 2010 controlled study from Brown University, bourbon caused worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level, but vodka still caused hangovers and both drinks impaired next-day performance about equally. The amount of ethanol you drink matters more than congener content.

**Is the methanol in alcohol dangerous?**

The small amount of methanol in commercially produced drinks is not dangerous at normal drinking levels. It may add to hangovers because the body turns it into formaldehyde and formic acid after the ethanol clears. Methanol poisoning is a separate emergency caused by illicit, homemade, or counterfeit spirits. Blurred vision, severe stomach pain, or confusion after drinking needs emergency care right away.

**How do you pronounce congener, and what does it mean?**

It's pronounced KON-juh-ner. The word comes from Latin and means "of the same kind." In general use it means a member of the same group or class. In the context of alcohol, it refers to the by-products in a drink other than ethanol.

**Does clear liquor give you a better hangover than dark liquor?**

On average, clear liquors like vodka and gin are lower in congeners than dark liquors like bourbon and dark rum, and controlled research suggests that can mean a somewhat milder hangover at the same amount of alcohol. The difference is modest. Drinking more of a clear spirit will still produce a worse hangover than drinking less of a dark one.

**Can DHM remove congeners from your body?**

There's no evidence that DHM breaks down congeners such as methanol, fusel oils, or tannins. Research on DHM focuses on how it may affect ethanol and acetaldehyde, mostly in animal studies with limited human data. It isn't a substitute for drinking less, and you should check with a doctor before using it if you take medication or have a liver condition.
